label: 1982–1983 El Niño

pois.caption_body: An altered jet stream drove relentless storm tracks across the southern U.S., triggering widespread and extreme flooding. The region faced significant inundation from heavy rainfall. Furthermore, Hurricane Alicia struck the Texas coast in August 1983 as a Category 3 storm, inflicting massive destruction and coastal erosion that resulted in $3 billion in total damages.

The atmospheric shift triggered a devastating, continent-wide drought. Acute water shortages fueled extreme dust storms and the catastrophic 'Ash Wednesday' bushfires in February 1983, which killed 75 people across southeastern Australia. Widespread livestock and crop losses devastated agricultural output and local economies.

On September 9, 1983, the historic, devastating Typhoon Ellen made landfall, prompting the Royal Observatory (now Hong Kong Observatory) to hoist the No. 10 Hurricane Signal. Hurricane-force winds reached over 200km/h, bringing widespread chaos, mudslides, power blackouts, and at least two deaths. Widespread marine incidents occurred as 24 ships were driven aground in and around Hong Kong waters.

pois.caption_body: The Yellow River basin experienced drastic rainfall deficits. Surrounding Jinan, extreme dry conditions severely depleted soil moisture and local reservoirs, devastating regional summer wheat and corn yields. This widespread agricultural failure inflicted heavy economic losses on millions of rural farmers.

pois.caption_body: Torrential flooding devastated this normally arid region, which received 11 feet of rain—a massive increase over the 6-inch norm. Floods destroyed infrastructure and triggered deadly disease outbreaks. Marine ecosystems were crushed when sea surface temperatures surged by 7.2°F in just 24 hours, leading to the collapse of the lucrative anchoveta fishery.

Warmer waters altered Pacific storm tracks, spawning Hurricane Iwa in November 1982. The cyclone caused $312 million in property and agricultural damage, leaving 94% of electrical users on nearby Oahu without power. The storm also directly resulted in the extinction of the Kauaʻi ʻōʻō bird.

Cooler waters in the western Pacific suppressed convection, triggering one of the most severe droughts in Indonesia's history. The lack of monsoon rainfall decimated crop yields and livestock, causing widespread famine and food insecurity. Economic damages from agricultural failure easily surpassed $100 million.

A southward drop in the jet stream drove a relentless series of severe winter storms into California. Catastrophic flooding, coastal erosion, and high winds caused 14 fatalities and roughly $265 million in damages. Furthermore, the anomalous oceanic warming severely stunted the growth and fecundity of the northern anchovy stock.

event_desc: One of the strongest ocean-atmosphere warming events in recorded history. Anomalously warm sea surface temperatures and reversed trade winds caused severe disruptions to global weather patterns and marine ecosystems. It triggered catastrophic flooding and extreme rainfall in the Americas, particularly Peru, Ecuador, and the U.S. Conversely, it induced severe droughts in Australia, Indonesia, and Africa. The global economic toll exceeded $8 billion, resulting in widespread infrastructure damage, collapsed fisheries, and thousands of fatalities due to floods, extreme fires, and disease outbreaks.

label: 1991–1992 El Niño

pois.caption_body: On May 8, 1992, torrential storms struck the territory, recording an unprecedented 110 mm of precipitation in a single hour—the highest hourly rate since records began in 1884. This intense deluge rapidly overwhelmed local drainage systems, triggering widespread urban flash flooding and multiple severe landslides across steep terrain, which heavily disrupted infrastructure and transportation.

pois.caption_body: The Yellow River basin experienced drastic rainfall deficits. Surrounding Jinan, extreme dry conditions severely depleted soil moisture and local reservoirs, devastating regional summer wheat and corn yields. This widespread agricultural failure inflicted heavy economic losses on millions of rural farmers.

pois.caption_body: Triggered the worst drought in a century across Southern Africa, ravaging agriculture. 2.4 million people (26% of the population) faced acute food insecurity as cattle died and crops failed. The regional drought affected 86 million people, necessitating the import of 11.6 million tonnes of relief food to avert massive famine.

Warmer Pacific waters fueled Hurricane Iniki in September 1992. Striking Kauaʻi with 145 mph sustained winds, it became the most destructive hurricane in Hawaiian history. The storm destroyed approximately 1,400 homes, severely damaged 5,000 more, and caused $1.8 billion in property damage, leaving 70% of the island's infrastructure ruined and three people dead.

Severe rainfall deficiencies started in March 1991, triggering a devastating multi-year drought across eastern Australia. By late 1991, a massive portion of Queensland was officially drought-declared. The relentless dry conditions decimated crops and livestock herds, ultimately costing the Australian economy roughly A$5 billion in lost rural agricultural production.

A severe drought, linked to the broader 1991–1992 El Niño climate shift, combined with civil war to trigger a catastrophic famine. The drought decimated agriculture in the typically fertile Jubba and Shebelle valleys. As armed factions plundered remaining grain, an estimated 200,000 to 300,000 Somalis died of starvation. Baidoa became the famine's epicenter, dubbed the 'City of Death,' where approximately 30,000 internally displaced people perished in September 1992 alone.

event_desc: A moderate-to-strong ocean-atmosphere phenomenon that significantly altered global weather patterns. While milder than the 1982–1983 event, it caused profound agricultural and economic disruption. It triggered the worst drought in a century across Southern Africa, leaving millions food insecure. Meanwhile, heavy rains struck the normally arid coastal plains of Ecuador. The altered jet stream brought heavy rainfall and sudden flash flooding to California. It also spawned catastrophic storms in the central Pacific, while causing severe drought and massive agricultural fires across Indonesia.

scmp_article.story_hd: Landslip warning as El Nino returns

label: 1997-1998 El Nino

pois.caption_body: The climate shift made 1997 Hong Kong's wettest year on record, bringing 3,343 mm of rainfall—51% above normal. This caused severe landslides and urban flooding. Additionally, altered ocean currents and temperatures triggered massive red tides (harmful algal blooms) in early 1998, wiping out thousands of tonnes of cultured fish and costing the local aquaculture industry HK$250 million.

El Niño-linked abnormal summer monsoon rains triggered catastrophic flooding across the Yangtze River basin in 1998. The disaster affected 223 million people, caused over 3,000 fatalities, and displaced 15 million. Floodwaters inundated 23 million hectares of crops and destroyed millions of homes. Total direct economic losses surpassed US$30 billion, marking one of the most severe natural disasters in modern Chinese history.

scmp_article.story_hd: Death toll rises to 250 after fierce storms

pois.caption_body: A severe El Niño-induced drought transformed traditional land-clearing fires into an unprecedented ecological disaster. Fires burned nearly 10 million hectares of forest, including 1 million hectares of carbon-rich peatland. The resulting toxic haze blanketed Southeast Asia, affecting 70 million people. Direct fire-related losses and haze damages across the region exceeded $4.5 billion, devastating local economies and global carbon sinks.

The typically arid coastal region was devastated by intense rainfall, receiving roughly 3,300mm—over 16 times its annual average of less than 200 mm. Catastrophic flooding destroyed bridges, roads, and agricultural lands, isolating rural communities and inflating local food prices. Furthermore, stagnant floodwaters catalyzed severe localized outbreaks of malaria, cholera, and acute respiratory infections.

Unprecedented heavy rains triggered massive flooding in northeastern Kenya, submerging roads and isolating communities. The sudden influx of water in the drylands bred ideal conditions for mosquitoes. This triggered a severe falciparum malaria epidemic with an attack rate of nearly 40% in Wajir, while a concurrent outbreak of Rift Valley fever decimated local livestock and worsened the humanitarian crisis.

Relentless El Niño-driven winter storms battered the region with extreme precipitation. Saturated hillside soils failed, triggering thousands of landslides across 10 counties throughout the winter and spring of 1998. The widespread earth movements destroyed homes, blocked major transportation routes, and inflicted over $150 million in direct property and infrastructural damage across the Bay Area.

A strong southern jet stream fueled extreme winter weather across the southeastern United States. Tampa endured unprecedented precipitation, recording a staggering 15.57 inches of rain in a single month. This extreme deluge inundated local infrastructure and agricultural fields, contributing to an anomalous severe weather season that included Florida's deadliest tornado outbreak in early 1998.

Extreme ocean warming fueled relentless rainfall and severe flash floods across coastal Ecuador. The extreme weather damaged thousands of homes, destroyed vital transportation infrastructure, and ravaged agricultural production. Socioeconomic losses for the country exceeded $2.8 billion. Furthermore, the widespread, stagnant floodwaters sparked severe outbreaks of water- and vector-borne diseases, including cholera and malaria, deeply affecting vulnerable coastal and rural communities.

Severe drought and El Niño-induced reductions in night-time cloud cover led to devastating, unusual August frosts. These extreme temperature swings destroyed staple sweet potato crops and wild food plants.

event_desc: One of the most powerful and destructive climate events in recorded history. Exceptionally warm waters in the eastern Pacific altered global weather patterns, leading to severe disruptions worldwide. It triggered record-breaking rainfall and flooding across Peru, California, and East Africa, spawning deadly disease outbreaks. Simultaneously, it induced catastrophic droughts in Southeast Asia, culminating in massive forest fires in Indonesia. Global economic losses were estimated to exceed $36 billion, with tens of thousands of fatalities and profound, long-lasting damage to ecosystems, agriculture, and infrastructure across multiple continents.

scmp_article.story_hd: Crops at risk as El Nino worries ripple across Asia

label: 2015-2016 Super El Niño

pois.caption_body: El Niño contributed to extreme temperature anomalies, making 2015 the warmest year on record at the time, with an annual mean temperature of 24.2°C. While 2015 saw a rainfall deficit, lingering atmospheric effects in 2016 brought a record-breaking autumn rainfall of 1,078.8 mm. This volatile shift culminated in the unprecedented issuance of a Black Rainstorm Warning in October 2016.

scmp_article.story_hd: Hong Kong sweating towards hottest year on record as El Nino and global warming take effect
El Nino effect: Hong Kong sees fewer typhoons and below half the usual rainfall for August and September

pois.caption_body: Northern and southwestern China experienced severe droughts and suppressed northerly winds, which severely exacerbated regional air pollution and caused dangerously high concentrations of PM2.5 haze.

An anomalous lower-troposphere circulation brought substantial moisture to southern and eastern China. This resulted in severely increased precipitation and devastating floods throughout the Yangtze River basin during the summer of 2016.

A severe drought gripped the country, heavily impacting the agricultural heartland of Mindanao. Below-normal rainfall affected over 60 provinces nationwide by early 2016. The extreme dry spell devastated crop production, pushing hundreds of thousands into food insecurity. Local authorities declared states of calamity across multiple municipalities as water sources dried up and agricultural damages mounted into the tens of millions of dollars.

El Niño-induced drought fueled one of the worst fire seasons on record across Sumatra and Kalimantan. Rampant peatland fires emitted massive greenhouse gases and blanketed the region in toxic haze. Millions were exposed to hazardous air quality for over two months. The prolonged dry conditions also slashed national coffee production by 20% and caused domestic rice prices to climb 25% above government limits.

scmp_article.story_hd: Out of control: Experts fear emissions from Indonesian fires could have ripple effect on atmosphere of the entire planet

pois.caption_body: The region suffered its most intense drought in the historical record, with an estimated return period of over 200 years. Massive surface water deficits severely suppressed groundwater recharge. Across Southern Africa, nearly 40 million people faced acute food insecurity as agricultural production collapsed and livestock herds were decimated by starvation.

El Niño brought anomalous heavy rains and severe flooding to East Africa, contaminating local drinking water sources with sewage. This triggered one of Tanzania's worst cholera outbreaks, with reported cases in 2015 and 2016 ranking as the second and third highest over an 18-year period.

Reduced cloud cover and record-high ocean temperatures triggered the most severe and widespread coral bleaching event ever recorded on the reef. The unprecedented heat stress decimated massive swaths of the ecosystem, fundamentally altering marine biodiversity and inflicting immense long-term ecological damage on the World Heritage site.

event_desc: One of the strongest ever recorded. It triggered extreme weather worldwide, causing devastating droughts in Southern Africa, Central America, and Southeast Asia, leaving over 60 million people food insecure and decimating crop yields. Conversely, it brought severe flooding to East Africa and South America. These climate anomalies created ideal conditions for deadly disease outbreaks, including dengue in the Americas and cholera in Tanzania. The phenomenon also induced record-breaking global heat, fueling devastating wildfires and causing unprecedented coral bleaching across the Great Barrier Reef.

scmp_article.story_hd: Climate change deal in Paris is crucial for Asia’s ability to thrive

label: 2023-2024 El Nino

pois.caption_body: El Niño contributed to making 2023 the second warmest year on record, featuring 54 'Very Hot Days.' It also fueled severe storms; in September 2023, Super Typhoon Saola triggered a rare Hurricane Signal No. 10. Days later, a phenomenal rainstorm dumped 1,067.1 mm of rain in September alone—more than three times the monthly normal—causing catastrophic urban flooding and severely disrupting the city.

scmp_article.story_hd: Hong Kong braces for another sweltering year, with 5 to 8 typhoons predicted

pois.caption_body: El Niño disrupted the East Asian monsoon, unleashing severe climate extremes. Following intense winter droughts in the southwest, the Yangtze River basin endured record-breaking summer downpours in 2024. The heaviest continuous rainfall since 1961 caused water levels to surge past alarm lines, ultimately bursting the Dongting Lake dike in Huarong County. The catastrophic flooding displaced thousands, devastated agricultural tracts, and severely damaged regional infrastructure.

scmp_article.story_hd: Floods move to China’s drought-hit farmland as Dongting Lake wall repair holds

pois.caption_body: The region endured an unprecedented drought, with the Amazon's rivers reaching their lowest levels since 1902. In September 2023, nearly 7,000 wildfires ravaged Amazonas state. The massive smoke plumes severely impacted over 2 million residents in Manaus. The extreme drought disrupted potable water access, halted river transport, and triggered mass mortality of fish and aquatic mammals, deeply affecting river-dwelling communities.

Southern Africa experienced its worst drought in over a century, prompting a national disaster declaration in Zambia. The dry spell destroyed roughly 1 million hectares of maize—nearly 45% of the country's total planted area. Agricultural losses were estimated at $804.8 million. Southern Province was exceptionally hard-hit, with 94% of its livestock farmers suffering profound impacts due to depleted water and pasture.

El Niño triggered devastating heavy rains and flash floods. In April and May 2024, the deluge caused the Nairobi and Athi rivers to burst their banks, inundating densely populated settlements. Nationwide, catastrophic flooding killed over 300 people, displaced 300,000, and swept away critical infrastructure. The disaster also ruined 24,000 acres of farmland and killed thousands of livestock, compounding regional humanitarian challenges.

Intensified by El Niño, the state of Rio Grande do Sul endured a series of historic storms. Catastrophic flooding struck first in September 2023 and returned with devastating force in May 2024. The extreme precipitation overwhelmed urban infrastructure and river systems around Porto Alegre, displacing hundreds of thousands of people, claiming dozens of lives, and causing billions in agricultural and property damages.

event_desc: A strong climate anomaly that amplified global warming, contributing to the hottest 12-month period on record. It triggered widespread, severe weather extremes. Catastrophic droughts struck the Amazon Basin, causing record-low river levels and massive wildfires. Southern Africa suffered its driest February in over a century, devastating agriculture and leaving millions food insecure. Conversely, East Africa, particularly Kenya and Tanzania, experienced unprecedented heavy rainfall and catastrophic flooding that claimed hundreds of lives, displaced hundreds of thousands, and destroyed vital infrastructure.

label: 1998-2000 La Nina

pois.caption_body: La Niña conditions fueled a highly unusual 1999 typhoon season. In September, Typhoon York necessitated the Hurricane Signal No. 10 for the first time in 16 years, remaining in force for a record 11 hours. Just prior, Typhoon Sam became the wettest tropical cyclone to ever affect the territory, dumping a record-breaking 616.5 mm of rain. The extreme storms caused immense flooding, hundreds of injuries, and significant infrastructural damage across the city.

pois.caption_body: The developing La Niña fueled an exceptionally active 1998 Atlantic hurricane season, spawning the catastrophic Hurricane Mitch. Striking Central America in October, Mitch stalled and dropped historic rainfall—unofficially up to 75 inches—over the region. In Guatemala, the cataclysmic deluge triggered massive mudslides and severe flooding that wiped out entire villages, devastated the nation's vital agricultural sector, and claimed hundreds of lives, severely setting back the country's economic development.

scmp_article.story_hd: Storm kills at least 801

pois.caption_body: The 1998–1999 La Niña winter slammed the Pacific Northwest with extreme maritime weather. Between 17 and 22 major storms battered the coastline, generating monstrous waves that peaked at 46 feet. This relentless barrage caused catastrophic coastal erosion, destroyed critical coastal infrastructure, and severely damaged marine and parkland ecosystems across Washington, Oregon, and Northern California.

La Niña conditions brought excessive rainfall to southern Africa, culminating in catastrophic flooding in early 2000. Compounded by Cyclone Leon-Eline, the Limpopo River burst its banks, completely inundating Chókwè. The disaster killed roughly 800 people, displaced nearly 463,000, wiped out massive tracts of arable land, and inflicted $500 million in damages, severely crippling the nation's agricultural economy.

La Niña-enhanced moisture fueled catastrophic torrential rains in December 1999, dumping over 911 mm of rain in just 52 hours. This triggered massive debris flows and flash floods along the steep coastal mountains. The 'Vargas tragedy' destroyed over 8,000 homes, killed an estimated 30,000 people, and caused nearly $1.8 billion in damages, marking one of the deadliest landslide events in modern history.

event_desc: The 1998–2000 La Niña was a protracted, intense cold episode that triggered devastating global climate anomalies. Emerging rapidly after the 'El Niño of the Century,' it delivered a catastrophic 'one-two punch' to global weather systems. The altered atmospheric circulation fueled torrential rains and catastrophic floods in Venezuela, Mozambique, and Bangladesh. Conversely, it induced severe, prolonged droughts across the southern United States and parts of East Africa. This multi-year anomaly drastically altered monsoon patterns, influenced an active Atlantic hurricane season, and caused tens of billions of dollars in economic and infrastructural damages worldwide.

label: 2007-2008 La Nina

pois.caption_body: Influenced by the same La Niña-driven atmospheric blocking that caused China's snowstorms, Hong Kong endured its longest cold spell in 40 years. From late January to mid-February 2008, the minimum temperature remained below 12°C for an unprecedented 24 consecutive days. The prolonged, gloomy, and chilly weather prompted continuous Cold Weather Warnings for nearly 600 hours, severely impacting public health and the elderly.

La Niña fueled an extreme convergence of cold Siberian air and moist southern air, triggering China's worst winter storms in 50 years. From January to February 2008, heavy snow and freezing rain devastated the region. The disaster destroyed millions of hectares of crops, caused massive power blackouts, collapsed roofs, and paralyzed transport during the Lunar New Year rush, inflicting roughly $21 billion in national economic damages.

scmp_article.story_hd: Snowstorm toll 111b yuan and 107 lives

pois.caption_body: La Niña significantly amplified the South American monsoon, unleashing torrential rains between November 2007 and April 2008. The ensuing catastrophic floods devastated the low-lying Beni region and surrounding departments. Nationally, the disaster affected over 120,000 households, caused 74 fatalities, and inflicted an estimated $511 million in damages—roughly 3.4% of Bolivia's GDP—severely crippling agricultural and livestock production.

A La Niña-altered jet stream created immense atmospheric instability across the southern United States. In early February 2008, this culminated in the catastrophic 'Super Tuesday' tornado outbreak. The violent storm system spawned 87 tornadoes across several states, severely impacting Tennessee, where 31 people died. The outbreak caused over $1 billion in damages and stood as one of the deadliest in modern U.S. history.

event_desc: a moderate-to-strong cooling of the equatorial Pacific that caused significant global weather extremes. It triggered one of the worst winter storm and freezing rain disasters in China's history, paralyzing transportation and destroying infrastructure. The altered climate patterns also caused catastrophic flooding across South America, particularly in Bolivia, while inducing severe drought conditions in Argentina. In the United States, a modified jet stream contributed to an unusually active and deadly early-season tornado outbreak. The event profoundly disrupted agriculture, claimed hundreds of lives, and caused tens of billions of dollars in global economic damages.

scmp_article.story_hd: Wild card named La Nina to blame for bad weather

label: 2010-2011 La Nina

pois.caption_body: La Niña amplified the winter northeast monsoon, making early 2011 exceptionally cold and dry. January's mean temperature dropped to 13.7°C, the lowest since 1977. The dry airstream heavily suppressed precipitation; 2011's total annual rainfall plummeted to just 1,487.2 mm, the lowest recorded since 1963. Furthermore, March saw a record-low mean relative humidity of 71%, significantly elevating local fire risks.

La Niña significantly disrupted winter precipitation patterns, triggering North China's worst drought in 50 years. In late 2010, Shandong received a mere 9 mm of rain—86% below average. The extreme moisture deficit devastated regional agriculture, heavily damaging 1.84 million hectares of vital cropland. Additionally, the acute water shortage left approximately 240,000 residents without adequate access to drinking water.

scmp_article.story_hd: Rain at last but no end to drought

pois.caption_hd: La Niña caused Queensland's wettest December on record in 2010, triggering catastrophic flooding. Rivers swelled to historic levels, inundating Brisbane and dozens of towns. The disaster claimed at least 35 lives, evacuated thousands, and severely impacted agricultural and coal production. Total economic damages reached roughly A$6 billion, prompting widespread disaster declarations and massive reconstruction efforts.

scmp_article.story_hd: Battered Brisbane seeks to bounce back

pois.caption_body: In January 2011, La Niña-fueled torrential rains triggered catastrophic flooding across eastern Sri Lanka. Floodwaters reached near 100-year highs, destroying the crucial paddy harvest and threatening regional food security. The disaster claimed 43 lives nationwide and forced over 360,000 people to evacuate. In the hard-hit Batticaloa district alone, roughly 95,000 families were directly affected, with thousands of homes obliterated.

A La Niña-altered jet stream deflected storm tracks away from the southern U.S., plunging Texas into its driest calendar year on record in 2011. The exceptional drought devastated the state's agricultural industry, causing over $7.6 billion in crop and livestock losses. The extremely hot, dry conditions also fueled historic, destructive wildfires that burned millions of acres.

La Niña suppressed moisture in East Africa, leading to consecutive failed rainy seasons in 2010 and 2011. This triggered the region's worst drought in 60 years. In Somalia, the extreme dry spell decimated agriculture and livestock, culminating in a severe famine that threatened millions with acute food insecurity and prompted a massive international humanitarian intervention.

The climate anomaly fueled Colombia's most devastating rainy season in 40 years. Continuous torrential rains from late 2010 to 2011 triggered massive flooding and landslides across 70% of the country. The disaster killed over 300 people, left 1.5 million homeless, and flooded over 1 million hectares of agricultural land. Economic losses exceeded $880 million, severely disrupting national infrastructure.

event_desc: The 2010–2012 La Niña was one of the strongest on record. It triggered widespread extreme weather by strengthening Pacific trade winds and altering global precipitation patterns. It caused catastrophic, record-breaking floods across eastern Australia, Colombia, and Pakistan. Conversely, the climate shift suppressed rainfall in the southern United States and the Horn of Africa, leading to historic droughts, devastating wildfires, and severe famine. Furthermore, the event contributed to an unusually active North Atlantic hurricane season while suppressing tropical cyclone activity in the Pacific.

scmp_article.story_hd: How La Niña’s icy grip may bolster China’s resolve in the South China Sea

label: 2020-2023 La Nina

pois.caption_body: La Niña contributed to an unusually active late-season typhoon period. In October 2021, Tropical Storm Lionrock and Typhoon Kompasu successively battered the city. This necessitated No. 8 Gale Signals with a record-short break of just 60 hours and 40 minutes between them. Kompasu alone brought over 100 mm of rain, raised water levels by over a meter, and caused severe flooding, roughly 900 fallen trees, and at least 20 injuries.

pois.caption_body: La Niña disrupted atmospheric circulation, contributing to extreme heat and severe summer droughts across southern China in 2022. The Yangtze River basin experienced record-low water levels, with Poyang Lake shrinking by over 70% of its surface area. The extreme drought compromised drinking water for millions, disrupted hydropower generation, and devastated autumn grain crops across the region.

China’s 2022 heatwave

pois.caption_hd: Amplified by La Niña and climate change, an intensified 2022 Asian summer monsoon triggered catastrophic flooding across Pakistan. Sindh was severely impacted, receiving nearly 800% of its normal August rainfall. Nationwide, floodwaters inundated one-third of the country, killing over 1,700 people, displacing 33 million, and inflicting roughly $30 billion in economic and infrastructural damages.

scmp_article.story_hd: Pakistan floods latest sign of climate injustice for Global South

pois.caption_body: Prolonged La Niña conditions suppressed rainfall, triggering a multi-year historic drought across southern South America. In Argentina, the 2022–2023 agricultural season suffered deeply, with wheat and soybean yields plummeting by over 40%. The severe moisture deficit, compounded by intense summer heatwaves, sparked widespread agricultural fires and cost the economy an estimated $20 billion in lost export revenue.

Drove relentless extreme rainfall across eastern Australia, culminating in catastrophic flooding in early 2022. Lismore was devastated when the Wilsons River peaked at a record 14.4 meters in February. The deluge inundated thousands of homes and businesses, leading to mass evacuations. Across the eastern states, the multi-year wet conditions caused billions of dollars in infrastructure and property damage.

Fueled the most severe drought in the Horn of Africa's recorded history. With five consecutive failed rainy seasons by late 2022, over 20 million people regionally faced acute food insecurity. In Somalia, the dry spell decimated millions of livestock, displaced over 1 million people, and pushed vulnerable communities in the Bay region toward famine conditions.

event_desc: The 2020–2023 La Niña was a rare, prolonged 'triple-dip' anomaly that significantly disrupted global climate patterns. By cooling the equatorial Pacific, it triggered cascading weather extremes over three consecutive years. It drove the longest and most severe drought in the Horn of Africa's recorded history and caused devastating agricultural droughts across southern South America and southern China. Conversely, it fueled catastrophic, record-breaking floods in eastern Australia and Pakistan, while also contributing to exceptionally active North Atlantic hurricane seasons in 2020 and 2021.

Asia set for supercharged heat as El Nino looms after 'hottest April' ever

label: 1957-1958 El Nino

pois.caption_body: In September 1957, during the developing phase of El Niño, Severe Typhoon Gloria slammed into the territory. The Royal Observatory was forced to issue the Hurricane Signal No. 10—the only time this highest warning was utilized in the entire decade. The storm battered Hong Kong with hurricane-force wind gusts exceeding 101 knots and torrential rainfall. The violent weather caused scaffolding to collapse, brought down power lines, and tore ships from their moorings, resulting in several fatalities and widespread infrastructural damage.

scmp_article.story_hd: Hong Kong typhoon: officer from stricken 1957 Dutch ship still looking for Chinese crewmates

pois.caption_body: Influenced by broader El Niño atmospheric disruptions, July 1958 brought unprecedented torrential rains to the middle and lower reaches of the Yellow River. The ensuing catastrophic flood saw the peak discharge at Huayuankou reach a staggering 22,300 cubic meters per second. The massive deluge devastated Henan and Shandong provinces, directly affecting over 740,000 people. The floodwaters submerged more than half a million acres of vital crops and obliterated roughly 300,000 homes, marking the river's most severe flood since 1933.

The Southern Oscillation shift heavily suppressed seasonal rainfall across eastern Australia. In 1957, the severe moisture deficit triggered widespread agricultural drought. The profound lack of rain withered pastures and depressed national crop yields, compounding the economic strain on rural farming communities before rains returned the following year.

The anomalous atmospheric circulation significantly altered winter storm tracks across the northeastern United States. In 1957, Ithaca experienced one of its snowiest years on record. The region received a staggering 115.1 inches of snow—representing 174% of its normal annual amount—causing significant disruptions to local transportation.

An El Niño-altered jet stream brought relentless winter storms to the American Southeast. This extreme saturation limited sunlight and promoted plant disease. Florida's vegetable farmers suffered profound agricultural losses, with winter bell pepper yields plummeting 31% below the long-term average and sweet corn yields sinking by 27%.

event_desc: The 1957–1958 El Niño was a strong, globally disruptive climate anomaly. Occurring during the International Geophysical Year, it became the first basin-wide El Niño extensively tracked by modern science. The phenomenon severely suppressed coastal upwelling in Peru, devastating the anchoveta fishery and causing mass starvation of guano seabirds. It altered the jet stream, bringing extreme winter snows to the U.S. Northeast and heavy rains that decimated Florida's winter agriculture. Furthermore, warm Pacific waters fueled a rare, destructive late-season hurricane in Hawaii and induced severe agricultural droughts across eastern Australia.

label: 1965-1966 El Nino

pois.caption_body: The decaying El Niño amplified moisture transport to southern China. In June 1966, this fueled a catastrophic rainstorm that dumped a staggering 161 mm of rain in just one hour and 518 mm in 24 hours. The extreme deluge triggered devastating floods and landslides across the territory, claiming 64 lives and inflicting over HK$5 million in damages. This tragedy directly prompted the creation of Hong Kong's first official heavy rain warning system in 1967.

scmp_article.story_hd: The day Hong Kong was hit by one of its deadliest rainstorms ever: in photos
1966 Hong Kong rainstorm leaves 64 dead in one of city’s worst floods ever–SCMP archive

pois.caption_body: El Niño weakened the East Asian summer monsoon and displaced the Pacific subtropical high, triggering one of the most severe droughts of the last 500 years in eastern China. The 1965–1966 exceptional drought ravaged North China, slashing summer precipitation by over 50%. The disaster affected more than 40% of eastern China's total area, profoundly devastating regional agricultural output and exacerbating rural food insecurity before expanding southward into the Yangtze basin.

The climate shift severely suppressed rainfall across eastern Australia, triggering a massive drought in 1965. The intense dry spell decimated wheat crops and forced significant livestock culling due to failing pastures. The drought profoundly impacted rural communities, slashing Australia's national agricultural output and contributing to widespread economic hardship before rains eventually returned in 1966.

Drastically warmed coastal waters triggered a phenological mismatch, severely reducing food availability (anchoveta) for marine predators. This caused a catastrophic mass mortality event for guano birds, with an estimated 15 to 17 million birds dying (nearly 76% mortality). Unlike previous climatic shocks, the seabird population failed to recover, permanently crippling the local guano fertilizer industry.

El Niño atmospheric shifts heavily suppressed seasonal precipitation across northeastern Brazil, triggering a severe 'seca' (drought) in 1965. The severe moisture deficit withered regional crops and decimated livestock in the semi-arid interior. The ecological shock exacerbated rural poverty, significantly damaging the local agro-pastoral economy and threatening the region's highly vulnerable, rain-dependent water resources.

El Niño severely suppressed the Indian summer monsoon, triggering a massive national drought. The acute moisture deficit devastated agricultural production, plunging national food grain yields by millions of tons. In Bihar, this triggered a horrific famine by 1966, pushing tens of millions into severe food insecurity and forcing an unprecedented dependence on foreign grain imports to prevent mass starvation.

event_desc: The 1965–1966 El Niño was a strong and highly disruptive climate anomaly. By severely weakening the Asian and Australian monsoons, it triggered catastrophic droughts across India and Australia, devastating agricultural outputs and culminating in the tragic Bihar famine. In the eastern Pacific, anomalous warming decimated the marine food web, causing an irreversible population collapse among Peru’s guano-producing seabirds. Furthermore, altered atmospheric circulations exacerbated extreme dry conditions in Northeast Brazil and parts of Southern Africa, significantly reducing global crop yields and underlining the profound socio-economic vulnerability of developing nations to the El Niño phenomenon.

label: 1972-1973 El Nino

pois.caption_body: The developing El Niño fueled exceptionally extreme summer rainfall. In June 1972, a catastrophic deluge triggered massive, devastating landslides at Sau Mau Ping and Po Shan Road. The catastrophe killed at least 138 people, marking the deadliest landslide event in Hong Kong’s recorded history.

scmp_article.story_hd: The deadly 1972 twin landslides in Hong Kong that claimed 138 lives in a day

pois.caption_body: El Niño severely weakened the East Asian summer monsoon, causing one of the worst droughts of the 20th century across northern China. The moisture deficit ravaged vital grain-producing regions, causing national grain production to plummet by roughly 10 million tons in 1972, exacerbating global food shortages.

Abnormally warm waters blocked cold, nutrient-rich upwelling, causing the total collapse of the Peruvian anchoveta fishery. The harvest plummeted from 12 million tons in 1970 to under 2 million tons by 1973, crippling the local economy and triggering a massive global shortage of livestock feed.

El Niño disrupted the Asian summer monsoon, causing one of India's most severe droughts of the 20th century. With food grain production plunging by 20% nationally, the Indian government launched unprecedented drought relief operations, employing over 5 million people in public works programs to avert massive famine.

El Niño-linked atmospheric shifts suppressed critical seasonal rains, triggering a catastrophic drought in 1972 and 1973. This immense moisture deficit catalyzed a horrific famine in Wollo province that claimed an estimated 200,000 to 300,000 lives, profoundly destabilizing the nation and contributing to the 1974 revolution.

The climate shift severely suppressed rainfall across eastern and southern Australia in 1972, culminating in widespread drought. Wheat production plummeted dramatically, dropping nearly 30% below average. The harsh dry conditions forced widespread livestock culling and compounded the global grain shortage.

Atmospheric shifts heavily suppressed seasonal precipitation across the Sahel, triggering the catastrophic 1972–1973 drought. The massive moisture deficit withered crops and decimated vast livestock herds. The ecological collapse triggered a horrific famine that forced mass displacements and claimed an estimated 100,000 lives regionally.

event_desc: A catastrophic climate anomaly that triggered a severe global food and economic crisis. Exceptionally warm eastern Pacific waters obliterated the Peruvian anchoveta fishery, disrupting global agricultural feed. The altered atmospheric circulation caused widespread monsoon failures and severe droughts across India, Australia, northern China, and the African Sahel. This massive simultaneous agricultural collapse caused global grain prices to skyrocket. The resulting catastrophic famines in Ethiopia and the Sahel claimed hundreds of thousands of lives, marking a devastating period in modern history.

label: 1973-1976 La Nina

pois.caption_body: La Niña conditions fostered intense western Pacific tropical cyclone activity. In October 1975, the exceptionally powerful Typhoon Elsie battered Hong Kong, necessitating the highest Hurricane Signal No. 10. While timely warnings prevented massive casualties, Elsie's extreme hurricane-force winds and massive 9.5-meter sea waves caused widespread disruption, capsized numerous fishing vessels, and injured dozens of people, standing as one of the most intense October typhoons in the territory's recorded history.

scmp_article.story_hd: Direct hit – but Elsie’s harmless

pois.caption_body: In August 1975, La Niña influenced the catastrophic Super Typhoon Nina, which stalled over central China and dropped historic rainfall—exceeding 1,000 mm in just three days. The unprecedented deluge caused the catastrophic collapse of the Banqiao Dam and 61 other reservoirs. The ensuing massive flood wave annihilated downstream towns, killing an estimated 150,000 to 220,000 people through drowning, subsequent famine, and disease, making it one of the deadliest natural disasters in human history.

The strong La Niña altered the jet stream, fueling immense atmospheric instability. In April 1974, this triggered the catastrophic 'Super Outbreak,' producing 148 tornadoes across 13 states in just 24 hours. Xenia suffered a direct hit from a devastating F5 tornado with winds exceeding 300 mph. The massive storm destroyed over 1,400 buildings in the town, killing 32 people, and significantly contributing to the outbreak's $600 million overall damage toll.

Amplified by La Niña, the 1974 summer monsoon brought unprecedented, torrential rainfall to the Brahmaputra River basin. The ensuing catastrophic floods submerged vast tracts of Bangladesh, destroying crucial rice crops right before harvest. In heavily impacted areas like Rangpur, this massive agricultural collapse combined with economic instability to trigger the devastating 1974 famine. The disaster ultimately claimed an estimated 1.5 million lives nationwide due to starvation and disease.

La Niña-enhanced monsoonal moisture combined with Cyclone Wanda to unleash catastrophic flooding in January 1974. Brisbane received a staggering 642 mm of rain in just 36 hours. The Brisbane River burst its banks, peaking at 6.6 meters and submerging thousands of homes. The disaster claimed at least 14 lives locally, left countless residents homeless, and inflicted roughly A$200 million (1974 value) in severe property and infrastructure damage.

The warm, La Niña-fueled western Pacific waters spawned Cyclone Tracy, which struck Darwin on Christmas Day in 1974. Striking as a Category 4 equivalent, the cyclone unleashed terrifying wind gusts of up to 217 km/h. The exceptionally destructive storm nearly obliterated the entire city, damaging or destroying 70% of all buildings. Tracy killed 71 people, left 25,000 homeless, and forced the largest mass evacuation in Australian history.

event_desc: The 1973–1976 La Niña was one of the most intense and prolonged cold-phase climate anomalies of the 20th century. With sea surface temperatures dropping over 1.0°C below average, it dramatically altered global atmospheric circulation. This multi-year anomaly amplified monsoon moisture, triggering catastrophic, record-breaking flooding in Australia and Bangladesh, which contributed to one of the deadliest famines of the century. In North America, the shifted jet stream fueled unprecedented atmospheric instability, resulting in the historic and deadly 1974 Super Outbreak of tornadoes. Collectively, the prolonged event caused devastating global economic damages, thousands of fatalities, and profound agricultural collapse.

label: 1988-1989 La Nina

pois.caption_body: The La Niña pattern fueled active western Pacific cyclone activity. In July 1988, Typhoon Warren battered the territory, unleashing extreme rainfall—including 459 mm locally within 24 hours. The deluge triggered severe flooding in low-lying areas like Sheung Shui, stranding residents and submerging over 100 hectares of fish ponds. The storm devastated local agriculture, drowning thousands of poultry and livestock, and causing extensive localized economic damages.

La Niña conditions created steering currents that drew intense tropical cyclones into southern China. In 1988, Typhoon Warren struck Guangdong, unleashing catastrophic flooding. The disaster destroyed 270 bridges, damaged numerous power stations, and completely inundated 178,000 hectares of agricultural land—including 68,000 hectares of vital paddy fields. The devastating storm caused 17 fatalities, over 150 injuries, and massive infrastructural collapse across the region.

A La Niña fundamentally altered atmospheric circulation, creating a persistent high-pressure ridge that blocked moisture from the central U.S. The resulting 1988 drought parched the Midwest, devastating agriculture. In Des Moines, spring rainfall plummeted to under three inches—just 30% of normal. Nationwide, the drought caused over 5,000 heat-related deaths, slashed corn production, and inflicted an estimated $40 to $60 billion in damages.

Amplified monsoon conditions triggered the worst flooding in Bangladesh's modern history. Massive river overflow submerged roughly 60% of the nation in the summer. In late 1988, an intense tropical cyclone worsened the disaster by striking the flooded coast. The compound catastrophe killed up to 6,000 people, destroyed 70% of harvestable crops, and displaced millions, sparking international debates on massive river control projects.

An unusual northward penetration of moist air fueled an unprecedented extreme storm over Khartoum. On August 4, 1988, the city received a staggering 210 mm of rain in just 24 hours—more than double its annual average. The immense flooding destroyed roughly 127,000 dwellings, leaving 750,000 displaced persons homeless, and triggered severe malnutrition and rampant diarrheal diseases.

Favorable La Niña conditions fueled a hyper-active 1988 Atlantic hurricane season. This birthed Hurricane Gilbert, which rapidly intensified to a Category 5 storm with 185 mph winds. Striking the Yucatán Peninsula near Cozumel, it forced 75,000 evacuations and caused catastrophic destruction. Regionally, the colossal cyclone killed 318 people and inflicted nearly $3 billion in damages across the Caribbean and Mexico.

Strongly positive Southern Oscillation Index values fueled intense Walker circulation, bringing exceptional moisture into Australia. By March 1989, vast tracts of normally arid inland Australia received record-shattering rainfall. The immense deluge caused widespread, catastrophic flooding, severely disrupting transport and profoundly transforming the arid ecosystem, eventually contributing to the complete filling of the enormous Lake Eyre basin.

event_desc: The 1988–1989 La Niña was an intense global climate anomaly that severely disrupted weather patterns. It drove a devastating multi-year drought across central North America and fueled the exceptionally destructive Hurricane Gilbert in the Atlantic. In Asia and Africa, enhanced monsoon and atmospheric shifts triggered catastrophic, historic flooding in Bangladesh and Sudan. Meanwhile, Australia experienced some of its highest rainfall on record, culminating in massive floods across its central and eastern regions. The event collectively caused tens of billions of dollars in damages, thousands of fatalities, and profound agricultural collapse worldwide.

label: 1954-1956 La Nina

pois.caption_body: La Niña significantly intensified the winter monsoon, bringing an extreme cold wave and exceptional dryness in early 1955. In January, the Observatory temperature plunged to 3.1°C—the lowest in 55 years—while the New Territories hit a record-breaking -3.1°C. This deep freeze was coupled with extreme drought and a record-low relative humidity of 21%, triggering severe regional water shortages and widespread frost damage to local agriculture.

La Niña intensified the East Asian summer monsoon, extending the 1954 'Plum Rain' season and causing relentless downpours. This culminated in the catastrophic 1954 Yangtze River floods, ranking among China's deadliest modern natural disasters. Historic water levels inundated massive tracts of the middle and lower basins. The catastrophic deluge killed roughly 30,000 people, displaced over 19 million, and caused colossal, widespread destruction to regional infrastructure and agricultural output.

In February 1955, La Niña-enhanced monsoon moisture triggered the catastrophic Hunter Valley floods. Maitland was submerged when the Hunter River shattered its previous record height by nearly a meter, peaking at 12.3 meters. The massive deluge killed 25 people, washed away 58 homes, damaged thousands more, and drowned nearly 100,000 livestock, inflicting roughly A$1.3 billion (adjusted) in damages.

La Niña conditions fueled an extraordinarily active 1955 Atlantic hurricane season. In August, Hurricanes Connie and Diane struck back-to-back, dropping over 20 inches of rain in some Northeastern areas. Pennsylvania suffered massive catastrophic flooding, with rivers cresting at historic levels. Regionally, the twin disasters killed over 232 people and caused nearly $1 billion in damages (1955 USD), destroying immense infrastructure.

event_desc: The 1954–1956 La Niña was a rare and prolonged 'triple-dip' climate anomaly that caused severe global weather disruptions. The anomalous cooling of the equatorial Pacific intensified precipitation across the western Pacific, triggering catastrophic and record-breaking floods in Australia and Singapore. In contrast, it altered the North American jet stream, fueling a catastrophic, multi-year drought across the central and southern United States, particularly devastating Texas. Additionally, it created favorable atmospheric conditions for an unusually active 1955 Atlantic hurricane season, leading to back-to-back landfalling hurricanes that brought unprecedented flooding and massive economic devastation to the Northeastern United States.
